title: The death of St. Eligius of Noyon
shortBlurb: The goldsmith who became master of the mint, chief councillor of Dagobert, and at last bishop of Noyon, died in his see on the first day of December 660…
body: Born about 590 at Chaptelat near Limoges, of Roman parents, Eligius — in French, Eloi — was apprenticed to Abbo, master of the mint at Limoges, and rose by his honesty: Clotaire II, pleased with the gold throne he fashioned, named him master of the mint at Marseilles, and Dagobert made his father's friend his chief councillor.

He used his influence for mercy, ransoming Roman, Gallic, Breton, Saxon, and Moorish captives, founding the monastery of Solignac in 632 under the Irish rule of St. Columbanus, and a convent at Paris where three hundred virgins lived under the Abbess Aurea. On Dagobert's death in 639 he left the court, was ordained, and about 641 was made bishop of Noyon and Tournai.

For nearly twenty years he preached to the still half-pagan peoples of the Scheldt and the Lys, built churches in honour of St. Martin of Tours and St. Denis, and buried with his own servants the bodies of executed malefactors. He died at Noyon on 1 December 660, and his feast is kept on the same day; he remains the patron of goldsmiths and metalworkers.

title: The death of St. Birinus, apostle of Wessex
shortBlurb: Sent by Pope Honorius to the heathen West Saxons, the first bishop of Dorchester died about the middle of the seventh century and was buried in his own cathedral city…
body: Birinus, a priest of Rome, asked of Pope Honorius I leave to preach the gospel to the idolaters of Britain; the pope commended his zeal and caused him to be ordained bishop. Landing in the kingdom of the West Saxons about 634, he found the people still pagan and stayed.

He baptized King Cynegils, the sixth in descent from Cerdic, who had founded the kingdom in 519, and with him many of his people; the king gave him for his see the Roman town of Dorcis, now Dorchester on the Thames. There he built and consecrated many churches and gained many souls to God.

He died on 3 December, in a year variously reckoned as 649 or 650, and was buried in the same city; Bishop Hedda afterward translated his remains to Winchester. The sees of Salisbury, Exeter, Wells, Worcester, Lichfield, and Hereford were afterward formed out of his single bishopric of Dorchester, itself soon transferred to Winchester, so that he is rightly named the apostle of Wessex.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 December

title: The martyrdom of St. Crispina
shortBlurb: A wealthy matron of Thagara, beheaded at Theveste in the Diocletian persecution, was named by St. Augustine with Agnes and Thecla among the glories of Africa…
body: Crispina was born at Thagara, in the Roman province of Africa, of a distinguished family, a wealthy matron with children. In the persecution of Diocletian she was brought before the proconsul Anulinus at Theveste in Numidia and ordered to sacrifice to the gods; she answered that she honoured one God only.

Her head was shaved at the judge's command and she was exposed to public mockery, but she remained steadfast in the faith, unmoved even by the tears of her children. Condemned to death, she thanked God and offered her head with joy; she was beheaded on 5 December 304. The acts of her examination, written not long after the event, are among the most precious documents of the age of the martyrs.

Her day was observed in Africa in the time of St. Augustine, who in his sermons repeatedly names her as famous throughout the land and worthy of the same veneration as St. Agnes and St. Thecla; a great basilica rose over her grave outside the city.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 December

title: France separates Church and State
shortBlurb: The law of 9 December 1905 ended the century-old Concordat between France and the Holy See and opened the age of laïcité…
body: On 9 December 1905 the French Republic passed the law on the Separation of the Churches and the State, ending the Concordat of 1801 by which Napoleon and Pius VII had for more than a hundred years governed the relations of Church and State in France.

The state would no longer recognize or pay the Church, but only associations cultuelles — associations formed in each parish for the conduct of worship; failing such associations, the property of the churches was to be lost forever and handed over to the charitable establishments of the communes. Two days later, on 11 December, Pius X lodged his solemn protest in a public allocution.

By the encyclical Gravissimo Officii of 10 August 1906 the pope forbade the associations, fearing they would furnish the state a pretext for meddling in the Church's inner life and the laity a constant temptation to rule the parish; the state then treated the old church corporations as nonexistent and transferred their goods, excepting only the edifices still used for worship. The Church of France was stripped of its endowments, and the law of 1905, much amended, still frames French laïcité.

title: The death of St. Finian of Clonard
shortBlurb: The master of Clonard, from whose school went out the Twelve Apostles of Erin, died on 12 December, mourned as the tutor of the saints of Ireland…
body: A native of Leinster, instructed in the faith by disciples of St. Patrick, Finian passed into Wales, where he conversed with St. David, St. Gildas, and St. Cathmael, and after some thirty years in Britain returned to Ireland about the year 520, excellently qualified, as Butler says, by sanctity and sacred learning.

He founded many monasteries and schools, the chief at Cluain-Eraird — Eraird's Meadow — now Clonard in Meath, which became a famous seminary; his Irish life reckons three thousand scholars. Out of his school came Kiaran the Younger, Columkille, Columba the son of Crimthain, the two Brendans, Laserian, Canicus, and Ruadan — the twelve whom old Irish writers name the Twelve Apostles of Erin — and their master was called the tutor of the saints of Ireland.

Chosen and consecrated bishop of Clonard, he lived on bread and herbs, drank water, and slept on the ground with a stone for his pillow. He died on 12 December, of the yellow plague as is commonly said; the year is reckoned as 549 by modern writers and as 552 by the Annals of Inisfallen.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 December
Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Apostles of Erin, The Twelve”

title: The death of Pope Adrian II
shortBlurb: The aged cardinal who had twice refused the papacy died on 14 December 872, five years to the day from his consecration, having for a season restored the peace of East and West…
body: Of a Roman family that had already given the Church two pontiffs, Stephen III and Sergius II, Adrian was seventy-five when the clergy and people of Rome chose him, much against his will, to succeed Nicholas I. He had been married before taking orders, and his old age was saddened by a domestic tragedy.

He followed closely in the footsteps of his energetic predecessor. At Monte Cassino he readmitted the repentant King Lothair of Lorraine to communion only after exacting a public oath that he would take back his lawful wife Theutberga; and against Hincmar of Reims he upheld the unlimited right of bishops to appeal to the Sovereign Pontiff.

At the Eighth General Council, which he convened at Constantinople in 869 and guided through ten legates, he effected the deposition of Photius and the restoration of unity between the East and the West. The Bulgarians he could not hold for the western patriarchate, but he seconded the saintly brothers Cyril and Methodius, and his endorsement of their Slavonic liturgy proved of enduring influence. He died on 14 December 872, exactly five years from his consecration.

title: The consecration of St. Eusebius of Vercelli
shortBlurb: The Roman Martyrology keeps on 15 December the consecration of the first bishop of Vercelli, the confessor whom Constantius banished for the Nicene faith…
body: Born of a noble family in Sardinia — his father is said to have died in chains for the faith — Eusebius was brought by his widowed mother Restituta to Rome, ordained lector by St. Sylvester, and in time called to Vercelli, whose clergy and people unanimously chose him for their bishop, the first of that see whose name is known. The year of his consecration is not recorded; it is commonly placed about 340, and the Roman Martyrology keeps its memory on 15 December.

St. Ambrose tells us he was the first who in the West united the monastic life with the clerical, gathering his clergy into one house to live almost as the monks of the East did in the deserts; his school gave many holy prelates to other churches.

In 354 Pope Liberius sent him with Lucifer of Cagliari to beg a free council of the Arian emperor Constantius, and at Milan in 355 he laid the Nicene creed upon the table and refused to condemn St. Athanasius; the emperor answered, 'Obey, or you shall be banished,' and sent him to Scythopolis in Palestine. Restored under Julian, he subscribed at the council of Alexandria in 362 immediately after Athanasius, laboured with St. Hilary against Auxentius of Milan, and died on 1 August 371, as St. Jerome's chronicle records.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 December

title: The death of St. Ado of Vienne
shortBlurb: The monk of Ferrières who renewed the martyrology of the Roman Church died archbishop of Vienne on 16 December, in a year reckoned as 874…
body: Ado was born about the year 800 in the diocese of Sens, toward the Gâtinais, of one of the richest and noblest families of that country, and was formed in the monastery of Ferrières under the Abbot Sigulph, where his humble obedience and love of study gained him every help in learning.

As a monk he visited the tombs of the apostles at Rome and stayed five years in that city. At Ravenna he found an old martyrology, of which he took a copy, improved it with many additions and corrections, and published it about the year 858 — the work by which the martyrology passed into the medieval Church. He compiled besides a chronicle, and wrote the lives of St. Desiderius and St. Chef.

St. Remigius detained him at Lyons and gave him charge of a parish near Vienne, and about 859 he was raised to the archbishopric of that see. He died on 16 December, having been bishop fifteen years and three months, in a year Butler reckons as 875 and most modern writers as 874; he is named in the Roman Martyrology on this day.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 December

title: Innocent III approves the Trinitarian Order
shortBlurb: By a bull of 17 December 1198 Innocent III approved the young Order of the Most Holy Trinity, vowed to the ransom of Christian captives…
body: St. John of Matha, with the hermit St. Felix of Valois for his companion, had gathered at Cerfroid, in the diocese of Meaux, a brotherhood unlike any then in the Church: its end was the redemption of Christian captives from the hands of the Muslims, by ransom, charity, and mercy.

Innocent III, though little in favor of new orders, as the Catholic Encyclopedia observes, granted his approbation to the enterprise in a bull of 17 December 1198 — the Operante divinae dispositionis clementiae — confirming the rule that John had brought to Rome.

That rule directed that the revenues of every house be divided into three parts: one for the brothers, one for the support of the poor, and one for the ransom of captives; each house was to comprise seven brothers, one of whom should be superior. The pope took the order under his protection, and the church of San Tommaso in Formis at Rome became its chief house. The Trinitarians, the first religious order vowed to the freeing of prisoners, spread through Europe and Spain in the later Middle Ages.

title: The death of St. Winebald of Heidenheim
shortBlurb: The brother of Willibald and Walburga and kinsman of Boniface, who ruled the double monastery of Heidenheim, died on 18 December, worn out by long sickness…
body: Winebald was the eldest child of St. Richard, a prince of the West Saxons and a kinsman of St. Boniface; with his father and his brother Willibald he made the pilgrimage toward Rome, and when his father died at Lucca about 722 he was of too weak a constitution for further travel, and remained seven years in the city at his studies, taking the tonsure.

When his cousin Boniface came to Rome in 738, he persuaded Winebald to share his labours in the conversion of Germany; ordained priest by that holy archbishop, he had the care of seven churches in Thuringia, especially at Erfurt. His brother Willibald, made bishop of Eichstätt, then called him and his sister Walburga out of England to raise the double monastery of Heidenheim, a pattern and seminary of piety and learning for the churches they had planted.

Afflicted many years with sickness, he said Mass in a chapel built within his own cell, and died on 18 December, in a year Butler gives as 760 and most modern writers as 761; after his death Willibald committed the monastery of monks to St. Walburga. The nun who wrote his life assures us that many cures were wrought at his tomb.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 18 December

title: The death of Blessed Urban V
shortBlurb: The Benedictine pope who dared to lead the papacy back to Rome died at Avignon on 19 December 1370, three months after his sorrowful return to France…
body: Guillaume de Grimoard, born at Grisac in Languedoc in 1310, a Benedictine professed at the great Abbey of St. Victor at Marseilles and one of the greatest canonists of his day, was chosen pope in 1362 while absent on an embassy to Naples, though he was not a cardinal; even as pope he wore the monastic habit.

Seeing that the States of the Church won back by Cardinal Albornoz would be undone if the papacy remained at Avignon, he left France on 30 April 1367 and entered Rome on 16 October, restoring the basilicas and palaces of his desolate city. There the western emperor Charles IV led his mule in token of humility, and a year later the eastern emperor John V Palaeologus abjured the schism and was received on the steps of St. Peter's.

But Albornoz was dead, Italy was restless, and his French entourage urged his return; St. Bridget came to Montefiascone to warn him that if he went back he would shortly die. On 5 September 1370, 'sad, suffering and deeply moved,' he embarked at Corneto, and he died at Avignon on 19 December 1370. Miracles multiplied around his tomb, and his cult was approved by Pius IX in 1870.

title: The martyrdom of St. Thomas the Apostle
shortBlurb: The apostle who touched the wounds of the risen Lord is held by ancient tradition to have died by the lance in India, his feast kept on 21 December…
body: Thomas, called Didymus, the Twin, a Jew and probably a Galilean fisherman, was made an apostle; his was the brave word, 'Let us also go, that we may die with him,' and his the confession wrung from doubt, 'My Lord and my God.'

Of his later preaching the ancients speak with less certainty. Origen, as Eusebius records, says that Parthia fell to him for his province; later tradition carries him beyond, to the Brahmans of India, and holds that he suffered martyrdom at Mylapore on the Coromandel coast, slain with lances — 'such was the manner of his death is the tradition of all the eastern countries,' Butler writes — though some of the learned, with Tillemont, place the Calamina of the old fathers nearer Edessa.

His body was carried to Edessa, and the Christians of St. Thomas in India keep his chief feast on the first of July; the Latins have kept it on 21 December, the day to which tradition assigns his martyrdom, in a year reckoned as 72. Digging at Mylapore in 1523, the Portuguese found a deep vault holding the bones of the saint, a part of the lance with which he was slain, and a vial tinged with his blood.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 December

title: The death of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini
shortBlurb: Mother Cabrini, who crossed the ocean to serve the Italian emigrants and founded sixty-seven works of mercy, died at Chicago on 22 December 1917…
body: Born in 1850 at Sant'Angelo Lodigiano in Lombardy, Frances Xavier Cabrini founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and, in loving obedience to Leo XIII, gave her life to the Italian emigrants of the New World. Her motto was the apostle's word: 'I can do all things in Him who strengthens me.'

Her works reached Italy, France, Spain, Great Britain, the United States, Central America, Argentina, and Brazil — schools, hospitals, and orphanages, sixty-seven institutions in all. Pope Francis recalls that she opened a house in the most infamous Italian quarter of New Orleans only a year after the cruel lynching of Italians there, and that she gave special care to orphans and miners.

She died in her room at Columbus Hospital, Chicago, on 22 December 1917, aged sixty-seven, a naturalized citizen of the United States since 1909. Pius XII canonized her in 1946, the first American citizen raised to the altars, and afterward named her patroness of migrants; a hundred years after her death Pope Francis held up her 'total and intelligent dedication' to the immigrants of her day.

sources.text: Pope Francis, Letter for the centenary of the death of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, 29 August 2017 (vatican.va)

title: The death of St. Servulus
shortBlurb: The palsied beggar of St. Clement's porch, who had never been able to stand or to lift his hand to his mouth, died singing psalms about the year 590…
body: St. Gregory the Great, who preserves his memory in the Dialogues and in a homily to his people, presents Servulus as the very figure of Lazarus in the Gospel: a beggar afflicted with the palsy from his infancy, never able to stand, to sit upright, to lift his hand to his mouth, or to turn himself from one side to another.

His mother and brother carried him into the porch of St. Clement's church at Rome, where he lived on the alms of those that passed by and shared what he could spare with other needy persons. He entreated the devout to read the holy Scriptures to him, and heard them so attentively that he learned them by heart, and consecrated his days to singing hymns of praise and thanksgiving.

When his sickness seized his vitals and he felt his end draw near, he desired the poor and pilgrims who had often shared his charity to sing sacred psalms beside him; then, of a sudden, he cried, 'Silence! Do you not hear the sweet melody which resounds in the heavens?' and so expired, about the year 590. He was buried in St. Clement's church, where his tomb was honoured with miracles, as the Roman Martyrology records.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 December

title: The election of Pope Clement II
shortBlurb: Four days after the Synod of Sutri, the Romans acclaimed Suidger of Bamberg as pope on Christmas Eve of 1046; on Christmas Day he crowned Henry III emperor…
body: In the autumn of 1046 Henry III of Germany crossed the Alps to receive the imperial crown and to end the scandal of three rival claimants to the papacy — Benedict IX, Sylvester III, and Gregory VI — seated, as it were, in St. Peter's, the Lateran, and St. Mary Major's. The Synod of Sutri on 20 December rid the Church of two of them, then adjourned to meet again in Rome on 23 and 24 December.

There Benedict, refusing to appear, was condemned and deposed, and the papal chair was declared vacant. The king, not yet crowned emperor, had no canonical right in the election; but the Romans, having no candidate of their own, begged him to suggest a worthy subject. Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen, positively refused the burden and suggested his friend Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, a man of spotless character; on 24 December the king took him by the hand and presented him to the acclaiming clergy and people as their spiritual chief.

Suidger was enthroned in St. Peter's on Christmas Day, taking the name Clement II, and his first pontifical act was to place the imperial crown upon his benefactor's head, on the feast on which Charlemagne had been crowned. He outlived his election only nine months, the first of the German reforming popes.

title: The death of Pope St. Dionysius
shortBlurb: The pope who gathered up the wreck of the Valerianic persecution and judged the great Dionysius of Alexandria died in the last days of 268…
body: A presbyter of the Roman Church under Pope Stephen, Dionysius had taken part in the controversy over heretical baptism, and Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to him as to an excellent and learned man. After the martyrdom of Sixtus II on 6 August 258, the violence of the persecution left the Roman See vacant nearly a year, until on 22 July 259 Dionysius was raised to it.

Some months later the emperor Gallienus issued his edict of toleration, which brought the persecution to an end and restored to the Church its buildings for worship, its cemeteries, and other properties; the new pope brought its administration once more into order. He is counted the first Bishop of Rome not to suffer martyrdom.

About 260 his Alexandrian namesake, writing against Sabellianism, expressed himself with inexactness concerning the Logos; the accusation was laid before the pope, who called a synod at Rome and issued, in his own name and the council's, a doctrinal letter condemning alike the error of Sabellius and the new error that separated the divine monarchy into three. He died on 26 December 268, as the greater number of authorities reckon; some give 27 December.

title: The consecration of Westminster Abbey
shortBlurb: Edward the Confessor's new church of St. Peter at Westminster was dedicated with great splendour on Holy Innocents' Day, 1065, days before the king's death…
body: A monastery had stood at Westminster at least since the tenth century — the tale of its church miraculously consecrated by St. Peter himself is a later invention — but Edward the Confessor resolved to raise it anew. Released by the pope from his vow of pilgrimage to Rome on condition that he should restore a monastery to St. Peter, he rebuilt the abbey church in the new Norman style.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that on the feast of the Holy Innocents, 28 December 1065, the king caused the church, which was entirely of his own building, to be dedicated with great splendour to St. Peter, the prince of apostles. Edward himself lay ill and could not be present at the service; he died on 5 January 1066 and was buried in his church.

Within days Harold was crowned there, and on Christmas Day 1066 William the Conqueror; every English coronation since has been kept within its walls. Henry III rebuilt it in the Gothic manner from 1245, raising over the Confessor's grave the church that stands today; Edward, canonized in 1161, was translated to his shrine on 13 October 1163.

title: The martyrdom of St. Sabinus of Assisi
shortBlurb: The bishop of Assisi and his deacons, who had made their glorious confession before the governor, gave their lives in the great persecution of Diocletian…
body: When the cruel edicts of Diocletian and Maximian against the Christians were published in the year 303, Sabinus, bishop of Assisi, and several of his clergy were apprehended and kept in custody until Venustianus, the governor of Etruria and Umbria, came to the city. Before him Sabinus made a glorious confession of his faith; the governor caused his hands to be cut off.

His two deacons, Marcellus and Exuperantius, were scourged, beaten with clubs, and torn with iron nails, under which torments they both expired. The acts, as Baronius and Baluze transmit them, tell that Sabinus had cured a blind boy, and that Venustianus himself, healed of a weakness in his eyes, was converted and afterward beheaded for the faith.

Lucius, the governor's successor, commanded Sabinus to be beaten to death with clubs at Spoleto, and the martyr was buried a mile from that city; his relics have since been translated to Faenza. St. Gregory the Great speaks of a chapel built in his honour near Fermo, and his name stands with his companions in the Roman Martyrology on 30 December, the day tradition assigns to their passion, in the year 304.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 December

title: The death of John Wycliffe
shortBlurb: The Oxford master whose writings prepared the English Reformation died at Lutterworth on the last day of 1384, struck down as he heard Mass…
body: Born probably at Hipswell, near Richmond in Yorkshire, in 1324, John Wyclif was educated at Balliol College, Oxford, resigning its mastership in 1361 for the living of Fillingham, and passing his years between the university and his parishes.

A Realist in philosophy who claimed St. Augustine for his master, he won influence in the burning questions of evangelical poverty and Church government; from 1374, when he sat on the commission sent to Bruges to treat with the envoys of Gregory XI, he stood allied with John of Gaunt's anti-clerical party, and his writings grew ever more severe upon the papacy, the religious orders, and the received doctrine of the Eucharist.

Probably paralyzed during his last two years, he suffered a second stroke in 1384 while hearing Mass in his church at Lutterworth, and died three days later, on 31 December 1384. The Council of Constance in 1415 ordered his remains to be taken up and cast out, which was done in 1428; the English Bible that bears his name and his Lollard followers carried his teaching into the age of reform.
